item.title: Stop trusting the database: signing your options table
item.dc:creator: demo
item.content:encoded:
Every WordPress hardening guide begins the same way: lock down file permissions, disable the theme editor, verify core checksums. Good advice. All of it protects the filesystem — and none of it protects the thing that actually runs your site.

The options table is executable configuration. active_plugins, siteurl, cron schedules, rewrite rules — a hostile write to any one of these changes what your site does on the next request, and every scanner you own will report green.

What a signature buys you

Not prevention. A signature does not stop the write; it makes the write visible. On every load, WordPress recomputes an HMAC over the sensitive keys and compares it to the stored one. Mismatch means someone changed the configuration through a path you did not sign.

add_action( 'init', function () {
	$keys = [ 'active_plugins', 'siteurl', 'home', 'template' ];
	$blob = wp_json_encode( array_map( 'get_option', $keys ) );
	$sig  = hash_hmac( 'sha256', $blob, OPTIONS_SIGNING_KEY );

	if ( ! hash_equals( get_option( '_options_sig', '' ), $sig ) ) {
		do_action( 'options_tampered', $keys );
	}

	// Every other admin-side write is unaffected; this only guards the boot-critical keys.
}
);

Twelve lines. The interesting work is in options_tampered: what you do when the alarm fires is the actual security design, building on the rotation habits from part 2.

“A file-integrity scanner watches the doors. The options table is a window that was never on the blueprint.”

Where to keep the key

Not in the database — obviously — and not in wp-config.php if you can avoid it. Part 2 covered rotation; the same discipline applies here. In part 4 we move the key to the environment and rotate it without downtime.

The database never lies, but it will happily repeat whatever you told it. That is the whole problem with trusting a table full of settings: the table remembers your intentions, not your outcomes. Somewhere between the two, most incidents are born.

I have rebuilt the same staging environment four times this quarter. Each time I promise myself I will write the setup down properly, and each time the promise survives about a week before the next deadline eats it. This week I finally wrote it down.

A junior engineer asked me yesterday why we still ship configuration as code instead of letting the admin panel handle it. I gave a long answer about auditability and rollback, but the honest, shorter answer is that panels drift and files do not.

There is a particular kind of quiet that settles over an office an hour after a deploy goes out clean. Nobody says anything about it, but everyone types a little slower, a little more carefully, as if speed were what caused the last outage.

Faith and infrastructure have more in common than most engineers want to admit. Both ask you to commit to something you cannot fully verify in advance, and both punish you for skipping the parts that felt unnecessary at the time.

My grandfather kept a ledger of every repair he ever made to the family car, in pencil, in a notebook that smelled like the garage. I keep the same ledger now, just in a repository, and I still smell like the garage by the end of most weeks.

The consultant's job is rarely to know the answer. It is to know which question the client has been avoiding, and to ask it politely enough that they can pretend it was their idea all along.

Every security review starts the same way: someone insists nothing has changed since the last one. Every security review ends the same way too, with a list of six things that changed since the last one.

I used to think the hardest part of writing fiction was the plot. It turns out the hardest part is admitting, three drafts in, that the plot you loved was hiding a better one you were too attached to see.

Business plans are just fiction with a spreadsheet attached. The spreadsheet does not make the story true; it just makes the story easier to defend in a meeting.

On Sundays I try not to open my laptop before church, and on most Sundays I fail by roughly nine minutes. The failure is smaller than it used to be, which I have decided to count as progress.

A cron job that fails silently is worse than one that fails loudly, because the silent one lets you build six more features on top of a foundation that quietly stopped existing three weeks ago.

The novella took me longer to finish than the novel that came before it, mostly because I kept mistaking brevity for simplicity. Short is not simple. Short is just short.

When a client says “just make it secure,” what they usually mean is “make it secure without changing anything I am used to.” Those two requests are almost never the same request.

I still remember the first time a signed commit failed on a machine I did not control, hours before a demo. The lesson was not about cryptography. The lesson was about which parts of my process depended on hardware I could not see from where I was sitting.

Faith communities and open-source projects both run on the same fuel: people showing up consistently for something that will outlast their own involvement in it. Neither survives long on enthusiasm alone.

The technology desk gets the loud stories, the ones with vendor names and outage timelines. The quiet stories, the ones about a schema someone refactored calmly over six weeks, rarely make the front page, but they are usually the ones worth reading.

I write serials the way I used to write status reports: one honest chapter at a time, with no promise that the next one will be easier than the last.

A ledger, in the old sense, was not just a record of money. It was a record of promises kept and promises still owed, and most consulting relationships are exactly that, dressed up in invoices.

The word “hardening” always sounds more dramatic than the work actually is. Mostly it means closing doors you forgot you had left open, one at a time, in an order that will not break anything else.

My editor once told me the best dialogue is the conversation two characters are having about something else entirely. I think about that note every time I write a scene set in a church basement.

There is a specific kind of business owner who trusts a spreadsheet more than they trust their own staff, and there is a specific kind of engineer who trusts a config file more than they trust their own memory. I understand both of them completely.

Opinion pieces are the easiest thing to write and the hardest thing to write well, because everyone already has one, and the only interesting move left is to disagree with your own first draft.

The verse I keep coming back to this year is not the one I expected. It found me during a week when nothing at work was actually broken, which made it easier to hear.

I have never met a migration that went exactly as planned, and I have stopped expecting one to. What I expect instead is a plan detailed enough that the surprises stay small.

A story about failover only becomes interesting once the primary system has already failed. Before that, it is just a diagram nobody reads until the night it matters.

The Consultant's Ledger series started as a single essay about a client who fired me and then hired me back eight months later. It turns out that story had at least four more chapters hiding inside it.

Writing about faith for a general audience means resisting the urge to explain everything. Some of it is only true if you leave the explaining out.

Every company I have consulted for has one system nobody wants to touch, guarded by a single engineer who has quietly become irreplaceable. Hardening that system is always more political than technical.

I keep a short list of sentences I am allowed to delete without asking permission from myself first. It has taken years to trust the list, and even now I ignore it more than I follow it.

The Quiet Ledger is not really about money. It is about the entries nobody wants to make, the ones that would force an honest total if anyone actually added them up.

Security work rewards patience over cleverness, most of the time, which is an uncomfortable lesson for anyone who got into this field because they liked being clever.

On the desks I keep, technology and faith sit closer together than business and faith do, mostly because both ask the same question: what are you willing to build on something you cannot see working yet?

A newsletter is a promise you make to strangers on a schedule you set for yourself, which is either the most honest form of writing or the most exhausting, depending on the week.

The Last Cron Job started as a joke about a script that outlived the company that wrote it. By the third draft it had stopped being funny and started being true.

I once spent a full afternoon arguing with a teammate about whether a bug was a feature. We were both right, which is the worst possible outcome for that particular argument.

Salt Water Wires began with a single image: a coastal town wired for a future that never fully arrived. Everything else in that novel grew out of trying to explain why the wires were still there.

The hardest part of running a small consultancy is not finding clients. It is saying no to the ones who only want a signature on something they have already decided to do badly.

A category count on a homepage is a small, honest number, and I have come to like small honest numbers more than large impressive ones that nobody can quite explain.

Every series I write eventually reaches a chapter where the characters know more than I planned for them to know. That is usually the chapter where the book actually starts.

The word “reconciliation” shows up in both my faith writing and my ledgers, and I no longer think that is a coincidence worth explaining away.

I read the API documentation twice before I trust it once, and I trust it once before I ever put it in front of a client's production traffic.

There is a kind of business failure that looks, from the outside, exactly like bad luck, and only looks like a decision once you have read the ledger closely enough.

item.title: Two working weeks a year
item.dc:creator: demo
item.content:encoded:
Forty minutes of CI a day, every day, adds up to two working weeks a year if you do the math. I did the math out loud at dinner and nobody at the table was impressed, but I was, and now I have to do something about it.

The annoying part is that none of the forty minutes is wasted, exactly. The pipeline runs the tests, builds the assets, deploys to staging, and waits for a health check. Every step earns its keep. It is just that half of those steps could run in parallel instead of in a queue, and I have known that for over a year and done nothing about it because the pipeline was not broken, only slow.

Tonight I moved the build and the asset compile onto separate runners and cut the number in half. Still two working weeks a year, spent waiting on a screen instead of writing. Just half as many as last month, which is the kind of progress that never makes it into a retrospective but adds up anyway.

My grandfather kept a ledger of every repair he ever made to the family car, in pencil, in a notebook that smelled like the garage. I keep the same ledger now, just in a repository, and I still smell like the garage by the end of most weeks.

The consultant's job is rarely to know the answer. It is to know which question the client has been avoiding, and to ask it politely enough that they can pretend it was their idea all along.

Every security review starts the same way: someone insists nothing has changed since the last one. Every security review ends the same way too, with a list of six things that changed since the last one.

I used to think the hardest part of writing fiction was the plot. It turns out the hardest part is admitting, three drafts in, that the plot you loved was hiding a better one you were too attached to see.

Business plans are just fiction with a spreadsheet attached. The spreadsheet does not make the story true; it just makes the story easier to defend in a meeting.

On Sundays I try not to open my laptop before church, and on most Sundays I fail by roughly nine minutes. The failure is smaller than it used to be, which I have decided to count as progress.

A cron job that fails silently is worse than one that fails loudly, because the silent one lets you build six more features on top of a foundation that quietly stopped existing three weeks ago.

The novella took me longer to finish than the novel that came before it, mostly because I kept mistaking brevity for simplicity. Short is not simple. Short is just short.

When a client says “just make it secure,” what they usually mean is “make it secure without changing anything I am used to.” Those two requests are almost never the same request.

I still remember the first time a signed commit failed on a machine I did not control, hours before a demo. The lesson was not about cryptography. The lesson was about which parts of my process depended on hardware I could not see from where I was sitting.

Faith communities and open-source projects both run on the same fuel: people showing up consistently for something that will outlast their own involvement in it. Neither survives long on enthusiasm alone.

The technology desk gets the loud stories, the ones with vendor names and outage timelines. The quiet stories, the ones about a schema someone refactored calmly over six weeks, rarely make the front page, but they are usually the ones worth reading.

I write serials the way I used to write status reports: one honest chapter at a time, with no promise that the next one will be easier than the last.

A ledger, in the old sense, was not just a record of money. It was a record of promises kept and promises still owed, and most consulting relationships are exactly that, dressed up in invoices.

The word “hardening” always sounds more dramatic than the work actually is. Mostly it means closing doors you forgot you had left open, one at a time, in an order that will not break anything else.

My editor once told me the best dialogue is the conversation two characters are having about something else entirely. I think about that note every time I write a scene set in a church basement.

There is a specific kind of business owner who trusts a spreadsheet more than they trust their own staff, and there is a specific kind of engineer who trusts a config file more than they trust their own memory. I understand both of them completely.

Opinion pieces are the easiest thing to write and the hardest thing to write well, because everyone already has one, and the only interesting move left is to disagree with your own first draft.

The verse I keep coming back to this year is not the one I expected. It found me during a week when nothing at work was actually broken, which made it easier to hear.

I have never met a migration that went exactly as planned, and I have stopped expecting one to. What I expect instead is a plan detailed enough that the surprises stay small.

A story about failover only becomes interesting once the primary system has already failed. Before that, it is just a diagram nobody reads until the night it matters.

The Consultant's Ledger series started as a single essay about a client who fired me and then hired me back eight months later. It turns out that story had at least four more chapters hiding inside it.

Writing about faith for a general audience means resisting the urge to explain everything. Some of it is only true if you leave the explaining out.

Every company I have consulted for has one system nobody wants to touch, guarded by a single engineer who has quietly become irreplaceable. Hardening that system is always more political than technical.

I keep a short list of sentences I am allowed to delete without asking permission from myself first. It has taken years to trust the list, and even now I ignore it more than I follow it.

The Quiet Ledger is not really about money. It is about the entries nobody wants to make, the ones that would force an honest total if anyone actually added them up.

Security work rewards patience over cleverness, most of the time, which is an uncomfortable lesson for anyone who got into this field because they liked being clever.

On the desks I keep, technology and faith sit closer together than business and faith do, mostly because both ask the same question: what are you willing to build on something you cannot see working yet?

A newsletter is a promise you make to strangers on a schedule you set for yourself, which is either the most honest form of writing or the most exhausting, depending on the week.

The Last Cron Job started as a joke about a script that outlived the company that wrote it. By the third draft it had stopped being funny and started being true.

I once spent a full afternoon arguing with a teammate about whether a bug was a feature. We were both right, which is the worst possible outcome for that particular argument.

Salt Water Wires began with a single image: a coastal town wired for a future that never fully arrived. Everything else in that novel grew out of trying to explain why the wires were still there.

A category count on a homepage is a small, honest number, and I have come to like small honest numbers more than large impressive ones that nobody can quite explain.

Every series I write eventually reaches a chapter where the characters know more than I planned for them to know. That is usually the chapter where the book actually starts.

The word “reconciliation” shows up in both my faith writing and my ledgers, and I no longer think that is a coincidence worth explaining away.

I read the API documentation twice before I trust it once, and I trust it once before I ever put it in front of a client's production traffic.

There is a kind of business failure that looks, from the outside, exactly like bad luck, and only looks like a decision once you have read the ledger closely enough.

Ordinary Time is the least dramatic season of the church calendar, and I have written more honestly about faith during it than during any of the seasons everyone else pays attention to.

The desk closest to the window gets the best light and the worst focus, and I have never been able to decide which one I need more on a given morning.
